Initial depletion of trace elements in animals and
humans is characterized by changes only in the metabolism
of the element itself in response to a suboptimal intake, the
individual target tissue compensating so that no disturbance
of biological structure or function are detectable by means of
a test. However, the individual usually complains of “lack of

energy.”

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: What are chelated minerals, and do they absorb better?
claims.answer_short: Chelated minerals wrap an amino acid around each mineral, absorbing ~40–65% — a 400% jump over metallic (8–12%); on a label they read as 'picolinate' or 'amino acid chelate.'
claims.answer: Chelated minerals - where an amino acid, protein, or enzyme is wrapped ('claw,' from the Latin) around each mineral - absorb far better than plain metallic ones: about 40-65%, which Wallach calls a 400% improvement over metallic minerals (8-12%). He notes the form was a 1940s livestock-industry invention (the original chelating agent, calcium EDTA, was a German pre-WWI antidote for arsenic and lead exposure, still used today for intravenous chelation of clogged arteries), and that you can spot chelated forms on a label as selenomethionine, chromium picolinate, or 'amino acid chelate.'
claims.verbatim:
Chelated minerals are approximately 40 to 65%
bioavailable, a 400% increase over the availability of metallic
minerals - certainly, a significant improvement over the


amounts elemental minerals that are absorbed.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: What is a colloidal mineral?
claims.answer_short: A mineral existing as ultra-fine particles (1–100 nanometers — 'nano-technology') suspended in liquid, too small to dissolve into single atoms the way salt does.
claims.answer: What is a colloidal mineral - and what does 'nano-technology' have to do with it? Wallach describes a colloid as a substance existing as ultra-fine particles suspended in a medium of different matter - so small (about one billion would fit into 0.01 cubic inch) that they cannot be seen with the naked eye. In the colloidal state, he says, the particles remain grouped together instead of separating into individual atoms the way salt does in a true solution. He notes colloids remain heterogeneous, multiphasic and insoluble as long as a larger number of the particles, if not all, stay within the colloidal size range of 1nm to 100nm - a range, he points out, known as 'nano-technology.'
claims.verbatim:
The interesting
thing about colloids is that they remain heterogeneous, multiphasic and insoluble at different concentrations as long as a
larger number if not all of the particles are within a range of
sizes of colloids (1nm to 100nm) known as “nano-technology.”

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Why can't you just swallow ground-up rock minerals?
claims.answer_short: Inorganic mineral particles are too large to cross the gut wall; only when amino acids convert them into absorbable 'crystalloids' can the intestine take them up.
claims.answer: Why can't you just swallow ground-up rock minerals? Wallach's answer: inorganic mineral colloids are 'too large' to pass through the gut wall or cell walls into the bloodstream. But in the presence of amino acids (from protein-containing food), a small percentage of them get converted into chelated minerals and organic colloids that CAN be absorbed through the intestinal membranes - this absorbable state he calls a 'crystalloid.' He adds that almost all nutrients are actually taken up by 'active transport' (the intestinal cell reaching out with a pseudopodium, a finger-like projection, to engulf the particle), not by passively drifting through a membrane.
claims.verbatim:
In the presence of amino acids, a small
percentage of the inorganic colloids form chelated minerals
and organic colloids which are able to be dialyzed through the
mucus membranes of the intestinal walls into the blood stream
- this bio-available mineral state is known as a “crystalloid.”

Crystalloids or organic colloids readily pass
through cell walls, while inorganic colloids are “too large.”

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Which form of colloidal mineral is best?
claims.answer_short: The plant-derived, living organic colloid — coated in a water-loving protein, up to 98% bioavailable — is the form Wallach favors over bare 'rock flour' or industrial versions.
claims.answer: Wallach classifies colloidal minerals into four forms that differ wildly in usability: (1) unprotected 'rock flour' - bare inorganic colloids from sea beds, clays and 'glacial milk,' which are really just metallic minerals and only feed plants (and only in healthy, microbe-rich soil); (2) organic mineral colloids from living systems (bacteria, fungi, green food crops, animals, humans) coated in a water-loving substance like gelatin, albumin or collagen - a 'crystalloid' with bioavailability up to 98%; (3) a carbon-coated form (a 10-12 carbon chain), thought to be the most stable natural type; and (4) an industrial form not found in nature, made by coating metallic colloids with sulfated castor oil. The second - the plant/living organic colloid - is the highly absorbable form his framework favors.
claims.verbatim:
The second type of mineral colloid is found in living
systems of bacteria, fungi, green plants (food crops), animals
and humans and is coated with a water-loving (hydrophilic)
substance such as gelatin, albuminoids or collagen. This
coating protects the now “organic mineral colloid” and allows
it to be a crystalloid for absorption, storage and physiological
uses and thus maximizing its bioavailability up to 98%.

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: What was colloidal silver used for?
claims.answer_short: Wallach relays older medical reports (not his own protocol): in 1917-18 colloidal silver was described as soothing inflammation and helping prostate/bladder irritation, itching, catarrh, even a post-childbirth blood infection. Silver sulfadiazine is still used in ~70% of U.S. burn centers.
claims.answer: Silver has a long clinical track record that Wallach relays from the older medical literature (presented for reference, not as his own protocol). Colloidal silver was reported in the British Medical Journal (Sir Malcolm Morris, 1917) as soothing rather than irritating - subduing inflammation and promoting healing - and used for enlarged prostate with bladder irritation, pruritus (itching) of the anus, perineal eczema, and hemorrhoids; J. Mark Hovell (1917) reported benefit for the Eustachian tubes, nasal-and-throat congestion (catarrh), and mouth, throat and ear infections; and T.H. Anderson Wells (Lancet, 1918) used it intravenously for a post-childbirth blood infection. Silver sulfadiazine (Silvadene) is used in about 70% of U.S. burn centers and stops the herpes simplex virus behind cold sores.
claims.verbatim:
colloidal silver is free from the drawbacks of
other preparations of silver, viz. pain caused and discoloration
of the skin. Instead of producing irritation, it has a distinctly
soothing effect. It rapidly subdues inflammation and promotes
healing of the lesions. It can be used with remarkable results
in enlarged prostate with irritation of the bladder, in pruritus
ani and perineal eczema, and in hemorrhoids.

claims.subject: aluminum
claims.question: Is aluminum in our food, and is that dangerous?
claims.answer_short: Unavoidable but normal, Wallach says: aluminum is Earth's most abundant metal (~12% of crust) and every plant takes it up - so no food or natural water is free of it.
claims.answer: Aluminum is everywhere in the food supply, and Wallach frames that as normal, not alarming: it is the most abundant metal in the earth's crust (12%) and is taken up by every plant grown in soil - so you cannot eat any grain, vegetable, fruit or nut, or drink any natural water, without ingesting it. He notes it is especially high in plankton and red algae and concentrates in mammals' hair and lungs.
claims.verbatim:
Aluminum represents 12%
of the earth’s crust and is the third most abundant element in the
earth’s crust and the most abundant metal in the earth’s crust.

claims.subject: aluminum
claims.question: Does aluminum cause Alzheimer's disease?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says no - he calls it a myth from 'a single faulty study,' citing later work (Oxford 1992, a 2007 German assessment) that found no proven dietary-aluminum link.
claims.answer: Does aluminum cause Alzheimer's disease? Wallach says no - and calls the scare a myth built on 'a single faulty study.' He cites the follow-up work: a 1992 study in Nature by Frank Watt and colleagues at Oxford, using a highly accurate technique, found the same aluminum levels in the brains of non-Alzheimer's controls as in Alzheimer's patients; a 1997 Berkeley newsletter and a 2007 German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment opinion both concluded there is no proven link between dietary aluminum and Alzheimer's.
claims.verbatim:
A single faulty study over 35 years ago suggested a link
between chronic aluminum exposure and Alzheimer’s disease.

claims.subject: obscure_elements
claims.question: What is actinium?
claims.answer_short: A naturally radioactive metal that glows in the dark like radium (its name is Greek for 'ray'). Wallach lists it among elements found in living tissue -- it gathers in bone and liver, where he speculates it may have a metabolic role, though he assigns it no health use.
claims.answer: Actinium is a naturally occurring (and radioactive) element that Wallach includes among those detected in living tissue. Beyond the physics - it is a metal that, like radium, glows in the dark, and its name comes from the Greek aktinos ('ray') - his biological note is speculative but intriguing: actinium accumulates in the bones and liver, where he suggests it may have some metabolic function. He also observes that plant roots readily absorb it, though little travels up into the plant. Presented for the curious; Wallach assigns it no specific health role.
claims.verbatim:
Actinium accumulates in and presumably has metabolic
functions in the bones and liver.

claims.subject: gold
claims.question: Does gold treat arthritis?
claims.answer_short: Wallach is cautious - doctors add gold to aspirin for arthritis, but he stresses it only helps ACTIVE joint inflammation, not advanced, destructive rheumatoid arthritis.
claims.answer: Does gold treat arthritis? Wallach reports that orthodox physicians frequently give gold compounds (gold sodium thiomalate, aurothioglucose) as an add-on to aspirin (salicylates) for arthritis when added pain relief is required, and he notes their reported limitation: gold has been reported effective ONLY against active joint inflammation, and is not usually helpful for advanced, destructive rheumatoid arthritis. He is describing and bounding an existing orthodox therapy, not putting gold forward as a broad arthritis cure.
claims.verbatim:
Gold compounds (gold sodium thiomalate, gold
thioglucose also known as aurothioglucose) are frequently
administered by orthodox physicians as an add-on therapy
with salicylates (aspirin) for arthritis when added pain relief
is required. Gold has been reported only to be effective
against active joint inflammation and is not usually helpful
for treating advanced destructive rheumatoid arthritis.

claims.subject: gold
claims.question: Is gold used to treat cancer?
claims.answer_short: One form is: gold-198, a short-lived radioactive isotope (2.7-day half-life), is used as radiation therapy for some cancers - a medical use Wallach notes, not nutrition.
claims.answer: Separate from gold's nutritional role, Wallach notes a purely medical use of a radioactive form of gold: gold-198, a short-lived isotope (half-life 2.7 days, made by bombarding natural gold with neutrons in a reactor), is used to treat some forms of cancer. This is radiation therapy, not nutrition - included for reference.
claims.verbatim:
A radioactive isotope of gold
with a short half-life of 2.7 days is used to treat some forms of
cancer. Known as gold-198, it is easily produced by exposing
natural gold to a beam of neutrons in a nuclear reactor.

claims.subject: bismuth
claims.question: What is bismuth used for, and did stress really cause ulcers?
claims.answer_short: Bismuth is the pink in Pepto-Bismol, used for stomach ulcers and gut infections for millennia. Wallach's myth-buster: ulcers were blamed on stress historically, but the real cause is Helicobacter pylori bacteria (Marshall & Warren, 1983) -- treated with antibiotics, antacids and bismuth.
claims.answer: Bismuth is not one of Wallach's essential nutrients, but he gives it a memorable entry. Chinese alchemists used it to treat gastric ulcers and gastroenteritis (stomach and intestinal inflammation) for more than 8,000 years, and today it is the pink liquid in over-the-counter gastrointestinal remedies like Pepto-Bismol. His larger point is a myth-buster: stress has historically been blamed as the cause of gastric, peptic and duodenal ulcers, but the true cause turned out to be infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori - a link Australians Barry Marshall and Robin Warren proposed in 1983 (and one already known in pigs back in 1952). His treatment of choice is a two-to-four-week course of tetracycline antibiotics, antacids and bismuth subsalicylate.
claims.verbatim:
Stress has historically been blamed as the boogy-man
as the cause of gastric, peptic, and duodenal ulcers. Animal
and human studies have in fact demonstrated that the true
cause of ulcers is an infection with a bacterium known as
Helicobacter pylori.

Australian gastroenterologist Barry Marshall, M.D.
and pathologist J. Robin Warren proposed their theory for the
bacterial cause of gastric ulcers in 1983. The bacterial cause
(H. pylori) for gastric ulcers was known in pigs in 1952.

claims.subject: obscure_elements
claims.question: Where does the word 'bromide' come from?
claims.answer_short: From medicine: sodium bromide, a bromine salt, was a common mild sedative in the late 1800s used to calm the nerves -- which is why we still speak of taking a 'bromide' to settle down.
claims.answer: A bit of history on bromine: sodium bromide (a bromine salt) was a common mild sedative in the late 1800s and early 1900s. That is where the old expression comes from - people still talk about taking a 'bromide' to settle down and ease stress and tension.
claims.verbatim:
Sodium bromide, a salt of bromine, is a mild sedative
that was commonly used in the late 19th and early 20th
centuries. People still speak of taking a “bromide” to calm
down and ease stress and tension.

claims.subject: carbon
claims.question: What is Wallach's view on global warming?
claims.answer_short: Off nutrition, he is skeptical of blaming humans -- calling our share of Earth's biomass 'pitifully small' and noting Ice Ages and warm spells have always cycled naturally. His fix is simply to plant more trees, which pull carbon dioxide from the air. (His personal stance on a debated topic.)
claims.answer: Outside of nutrition, Wallach shares his personal view on climate. He is skeptical of blaming human activity for global warming - he calls humanity's share of the planet's biomass 'pitifully small' and argues that Ice Ages and warm periods have cycled naturally throughout Earth's history, so today's warming is part of that long-running cycle. His proposed remedy is simply to plant more trees, which pull carbon dioxide from the air and release oxygen and water.
claims.verbatim:
While many individuals and organizations, want to
blame man’s activities and pitifully small biomass for “global
warming,” we must look to the past for the cycles of Ice Ages and
“global warming” that have taken place over and over through
the millennia to understand the cyclic nature of these events.

claims.subject: macronutrients
claims.question: What are carbohydrates?
claims.answer_short: The body's convenient fuel (but not essential) - plants build them from CO2 and water by photosynthesis. Sized as single sugars, double sugars, and long chains like starch and fiber.
claims.answer: What are carbohydrates? Wallach explains that carbs and sugars are the body's convenient everyday fuel, but - importantly - they are NOT essential nutrients: the body can make all the carbohydrate it needs by reconfiguring proteins and fats. Plants build carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight (photosynthesis, which runs on chlorophyll, a magnesium/carbon ring). Carbohydrates are classified by size: single sugars (monosaccharides like glucose and fructose), double sugars (disaccharides like sucrose, maltose and lactose), and large chains (polysaccharides like starch, cellulose, fiber and glycogen).
claims.verbatim:
While
carbohydrates and sugars are convenient sources of fuel for
energy, they are not essential nutrients as all living organisms
can make them by reconfiguring proteins and fats.

claims.subject: macronutrients
claims.question: What are fats?
claims.answer_short: Water-repelling molecules packing ~9 calories a gram (vs 4.5); mostly triglycerides (glycerol + fatty acids). Fatty acids differ by chain length, saturation, and 'omega' number.
claims.answer: A primer on fats: like carbohydrates, fats (lipids) are built from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, but they don't dissolve in water and pack more energy - about 9 calories per gram versus 4.5 for carbohydrate or protein. The main form of fat is the triglyceride: a molecule of glycerol joined to fatty acids. Fatty acids are described three ways - chain length (short, medium or long, by the number of carbons), how 'saturated' they are with hydrogen (no double bonds = saturated; one = monounsaturated; several = polyunsaturated), and where the first double bond sits counting from the tail (the 'omega' number, e.g. omega-3, omega-6).
claims.verbatim:
Triglycerides (the primary component of fats and oils)
are composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Structurally,
they are esters of a trihydric alcohol (glycerol) and fatty acids.

claims.subject: cholesterol
claims.question: What does cholesterol actually do in the body?
claims.answer_short: It's the raw material for vitamin D, bile acids, and the adrenal stress and sex hormones — so a cholesterol deficiency can worsen menopause and flatten libido.
claims.answer: Is cholesterol bad for you? Wallach's answer is emphatically no - it is essential. It is a structural part of every cell membrane and of the myelin that insulates the brain and spinal cord, and it is the raw material the body uses to make vitamin D, bile acids (which digest fat), the adrenal stress hormones, and the sex hormones estrogen, progesterone and testosterone. Because of that hormone role, he warns that a cholesterol deficiency can make menopause miserable for women and can flatten a man's sex drive.
claims.verbatim:
Cholesterol is an essential part of the structure of cell walls,
brain and spinal cord (myelin), the raw material for the
production of vitamin D in the human body, bile acids, adrenal
cortical hormones, estrogens (a cholesterol deficiency makes
menopause a living hell), progesterone, and testosterone (a
cholesterol deficiency will turn hubby into a TV watching
steer who is totally disinterested in sex).

claims.subject: macronutrients
claims.question: What are proteins?
claims.answer_short: The body's most abundant carbon compound - the main stuff of muscle and every cell, and enzymes are proteins too. Built from amino acids linked by peptide bonds; they add nitrogen.
claims.answer: What are proteins? Like carbohydrates and fats they contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, but proteins add nitrogen (about 16%, the 'amine' group), sometimes with phosphorus, iron, sulfur or cobalt. Their basic building block is the amino acid; amino acids link by 'peptide bonds' into long chains, and digestion breaks those bonds to free the individual amino acids again. Proteins are the most abundant carbon-based compound in the body - the main stuff of muscle and every cell - and enzymes (the workers that speed up the body's chemical reactions) are themselves proteins.
claims.verbatim:
Proteins are the fundamental structural components
of the living cell (cytoplasm). They are essential parts of the
cell nucleus and protoplasm. Proteins are the most abundant
of all carbon containing organic compounds in the human
body.

claims.subject: macronutrients
claims.question: Can you eat too much protein?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's view: a healthy person can eat even 300 g of protein a day (nearly 3/4 lb of meat) with no harm - as long as they have no kidney or liver disease and supplement properly.
claims.answer: Can you eat too much protein? Wallach's view: a healthy person can consume even 300 grams of protein a day - nearly three-quarters of a pound of meat - with no ill effects, as long as they do not have kidney or liver disease and they supplement properly with vitamins and minerals.
claims.verbatim:
An individual consuming protein at even 300 gm per
day (almost 3/4 of a pound of meat a day) will have no adverse
effects as long as they do not have kidney or liver disease and
supplement properly with vitamins and minerals.

claims.subject: amino_acids
claims.question: What does each amino acid do?
claims.answer_short: Many build protein (valine, lysine, leucine...); tryptophan makes niacin and serotonin; phenylalanine makes thyroid hormone and adrenaline; methionine makes choline and creatine.
claims.answer: Wallach's essential amino acids and what each does. Classically there are nine that must come from the diet because the body cannot make them, and Wallach would add three more - arginine, taurine and tyrosine. Their roles: valine, lysine, threonine, leucine and isoleucine build protein; tryptophan is the precursor of niacin (vitamin B3) and serotonin; phenylalanine makes thyroxine (a thyroid hormone) and epinephrine (adrenaline); methionine makes choline and creatine phosphate; histidine makes histamine; and the added three help prevent specific diseases (arginine, taurine, tyrosine - see the related claim).
claims.verbatim:
Classically there are nine essential amino acids that are
required in the daily diet as they cannot be manufactured by
the human body.

claims.subject: vitamins
claims.question: What are vitamins?
claims.answer_short: Organic compounds the body needs in tiny daily amounts but can't make itself; they work mostly as coenzymes (switching enzymes on) and supply no calories and no body mass.
claims.answer: What are vitamins? Wallach defines them as a group of unrelated, carbon-based organic compounds the body needs in tiny daily amounts for specific chemical reactions - essential for normal growth, development, maintenance, health, longevity and life itself. They work mainly as coenzymes (helper molecules that switch enzymes on) and cannot be manufactured by the human body, yet they supply no calories and add no body mass. Getting optimal vitamins, he says, goes a long way toward preventing birth defects and many debilitating degenerative diseases.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamins are essential nutrients in that, they can not
be manufactured by humans; they do not supply calories or
contribute to body mass.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: How much calcium are humans designed to eat?
claims.answer_short: Wallach argues we're built for Stone-Age intakes of 1,600–3,000 mg a day; modern Americans get a fraction — as little as 300 mg.
claims.answer: Wallach argues humans are biologically designed to eat high-calcium diets. In the late Paleolithic (35,000–10,000 years ago), wild plant foods and game supplied about 1,600 mg of calcium a day at rest and 2,000–3,000 mg at the activity levels of hunting and labor. The agricultural revolution ~10,000 years ago narrowed the variety of foods and permanently lowered mineral intake — by the 20th century American adults took in only one-fifth to one-third as much, a median of 300–508 mg/day for women and 680 mg/day for men (National Health & Nutrition Examination Survey II).
claims.verbatim:
The
uncultivated food plants and wild game commonly available
to Stone Age humans would supply 1600 mg of calcium at
basal energy intakes and between 2,000 and 3,000 mg of
calcium at the energy levels required to support hunting and
work.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: How much calcium is in your body, and where?
claims.answer_short: Calcium is the body's most abundant mineral (~1–1.2 kg); 99% sits in the bones and teeth, and the last 1% works in blood and cells.
claims.answer: Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body. The average man holds 1,200 grams and the average woman 1,000 grams — 2% of adult body weight, and up to 39% of the body's total mineral reserves (the ash left after cremation). Ninety-nine percent of it sits in the bones and teeth; the remaining 1% circulates in blood, extracellular fluid and inside cells, where it acts as a cofactor and activator for numerous enzyme systems.
claims.verbatim:
Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human
body. The average male has 1,200 grams and the average
female has 1,000 grams. Calcium makes up two percent of the
adult body weight (water makes up 65 to 75%). Calcium also
composes up to 39% of the total mineral reserves (ash after
cremation). Ninety-nine percent of body calcium is found in
bones and teeth. The other one percent is found in the blood,
extracellular fluids, and within cells where it is a cofactor and
activator for numerous enzyme systems.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: How is calcium stored in your bones?
claims.answer_short: As hydroxyapatite crystals on a protein 'bone matrix' — soak a bone in vinegar two weeks and the calcium leaches out, leaving the bendy scaffold.
claims.answer: In bone, calcium is stored as hydroxyapatite salts (calcium phosphate plus calcium carbonate) laid down in a crystal lattice bound to a protein scaffold called the "bone matrix." Wallach offers a simple demonstration of that matrix: put a chicken "drumstick" bone in a quart of vinegar for two weeks and the calcium is leached out of the bone, leaving the protein matrix behind.
claims.verbatim:
in a classic crystal structure bound to a protein framework
called “bone matrix.”

To extract the calcium from a bone and reveal the
protein matrix, put a chicken “drumstick” bone in a quart of
vinegar for two weeks and the calcium will be leached out of
the bone leaving the protein matrix.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: What does calcium do besides build bone?
claims.answer_short: It's a working cofactor: it releases ATP energy for muscle, drives blood clotting, moves signals across membranes, fires nerves and paces the heartbeat.
claims.answer: Beyond its structural role, calcium is a working cofactor throughout the body. It is required to release energy from ATP (adenosine triphosphate) for muscle contraction, and it is a required cofactor in blood clotting: ionized calcium stimulates platelets to release thromboplastin and converts prothrombin to thrombin, which helps convert fibrinogen into fibrin — the protein web that traps red blood cells to form a clot. Calcium also mediates transport across cell and organelle membranes, affects the release of neurotransmitters at synapses, mediates the synthesis, secretion and metabolic effects of hormones and enzymes, and helps regulate the rate and strength of the heartbeat, muscle tone and how receptive muscle is to nerve stimulation.
claims.verbatim:
In addition to being a major structural mineral, Ca is also
required as a cofactor for the release of energy from ATP for
muscular contraction, and blood clotting. In the blood clotting
process, ionized Ca stimulates the release of thromboplastin
from platelets and converts prothrombin to thrombin. Thrombin
helps to convert fibrinogen to fibrin, and fibrin is the protein
web that traps red blood cells to create blood clots.

claims.subject: absorption
claims.question: What blocks calcium from being absorbed?
claims.answer_short: It depends on the form and the gut: a metallic calcium pill may be only 1–3% absorbed, and phytates in grains, low stomach acid, celiac damage, sugar and carbonation all drive it lower.
claims.answer: How well calcium is absorbed depends heavily on its form and the gut environment. It is taken up mainly in the duodenum while the contents are still acidic; once the intestine turns alkaline, absorption falls off. Plain metallic calcium may be only 1-3% absorbed, whereas an organically bound, plant-derived colloidal or water-soluble chelated form can reach up to 98%. Wallach lists the causes of a calcium deficiency as: too little vitamin D; low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria, which can follow a salt-restricted diet); lactose intolerance; celiac disease; a high-fat or low-protein diet; and heavy fiber and phytate intake. Phytic acid (in grain bran, oatmeal, whole wheat) and oxalic acid (in rhubarb, spinach, chard, mustard greens) each bind calcium into insoluble, unabsorbable salts, and excess sugar, carbonation and caffeine leach stored calcium from the bones.
claims.verbatim:
Causes of a calcium deficiency can include, a
deficiency or lack of vitamin D; the lack of stomach acid
or hypochlorhydria can result from a restricted NaCl (salt)
intake; lactose intolerance; celiac disease; high fat diet; low
protein diet; and a high fiber and phytate consumption.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: How does the body keep blood calcium steady?
claims.answer_short: Two hormones — parathormone and calcitonin — hold serum calcium at 8.5–10.5 mg/dL, mostly by borrowing it from and returning it to bone.
claims.answer: The body holds blood calcium within a tight range using two hormones. Parathormone (from the parathyroid glands) and calcitonin (from the thyroid) keep serum calcium at 8.5-10.5 mg/dL, largely by drawing on the calcium reserves in bone. Parathormone raises blood calcium — pulling it from bone, making the kidney retain more, and making the gut absorb more efficiently; when blood calcium climbs above 10.5 mg/dL from too much parathyroid activity, calcitonin reduces how much calcium is released from the bones.
claims.verbatim:
Under optimal conditions, parathormone secreted by
the parathyroid gland and calcitonin secreted by the thyroid
gland, maintain a serum calcium of 8.5 to 10.5 mg% by drawing
on calcium reserves from the bones.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: What in the modern diet drains your calcium?
claims.answer_short: Fiber, salt and soft-drink phosphate force calcium out of the body — the modern diet's calcium-to-phosphorus ratio simply can't be met by eating alone.
claims.answer: Several common features of the modern diet quietly raise the body's calcium requirement — an increased calcium "cost." Overloading on fiber, salt and phosphates (soft drinks) all force more calcium out: urinary calcium loss rose from 96 mg to 148 mg per day when food was heavily salted, and doubling phosphate intake raised urinary calcium output by 50%. Wallach argues the industrialized diet is chronically calcium-poor and phosphorus-rich, so the ideal calcium-to-phosphorus (Ca:P) ratio of 2:1 is impossible to hit by eating alone (you would have to eat 25 pounds of broccoli for every 16 oz T-bone steak); the only practical route is to avoid high-phosphorus foods and supplement with plant-derived colloidal and chelated calcium.
claims.verbatim:
Other nutrients that are commonly found in the
American diet can aggravate the national calcium deficiency
crisis. Diets rich with an overabundance of fiber, salt and
phosphates (soft drinks) result in an increased calcium “cost.”
In effect, these foods increase the dietary requirements for
calcium. Urinary calcium loss increased from 96 mg per day
to 148 mg per day when food was excessively salted. As


 

phosphate intake is doubled, the output of urinary calcium
increases by 50%.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: How many diseases does Wallach tie to calcium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: 147 — Wallach links no fewer than 147 diseases to calcium deficiency or imbalance, and says U.S. diets are so deficient that only supplements fix it.
claims.answer: Wallach holds that there are no fewer than 147 deficiency diseases attributable to calcium deficiencies or imbalances, and that American diets across the board are critically deficient in calcium — so the only practical way to get enough is supplementation. He jabs at the researchers who studied the problem: instead of recommending effective calcium supplementation, they told people to eat five cups of broccoli a day ("Try and get a kid to eat five cups of broccoli each day").
claims.verbatim:
There are no less than 147 deficiency diseases that can
be attributed to calcium deficiencies or imbalances. The most
recent clinical research clearly points out that the entire scope
of American diets are critically deficient in calcium. The only
practical way to obtain enough sufficient amounts of calcium
is through supplementation.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Which famous people did Wallach say had calcium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: He points to Pope John Paul II, Elizabeth Taylor, 'Bo' Jackson and vegan NBA star Bill Walton — all, he says, with osteoporosis or fractures.
claims.answer: To make the point that calcium deficiency reaches even the famous and well-fed, Wallach lists public figures he says suffered an advanced degree of it: Pope John Paul II (fractured hip / osteoporosis), Elizabeth Taylor (osteoporosis / multiple hip-replacement surgeries), "Bo" Jackson (fractured hip / osteoporosis), and Bill Walton, a vegan of professional-basketball fame (osteoporosis, arthritis, fractures).
claims.verbatim:
Famous people who have suffered from an advanced
degree of calcium deficiency include Pope John Paul II
(fractured hip/ osteoporosis), Elizabeth Taylor (osteoporosis/
multiple hip replacement surgeries), “Bo” Jackson (fractured
hip/osteoporosis), Bill Walton, a vegan of professional
basketball fame (osteoporosis, arthritis, fractures), etc.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: What does cobalt have to do with vitamin B12?
claims.answer_short: Cobalt is the heart of vitamin B12 -- it sits in a ring related to the ones holding iron in hemoglobin and magnesium in chlorophyll, and gives B12 its red color. 'Cyanocobalamine' was named for a cyanide group on the first B12 isolated (1948).
claims.answer: Some biochemistry of vitamin B12: its cobalt sits chelated in a large tetrapyrrole ring — the same ring family as the porphyrin ring that holds iron in hemoglobin and magnesium in chlorophyll. The first B12 molecule isolated in the lab carried a cyanide group, hence the name cyanocobalamine; several cobalamine forms have B12 activity, with cyanocobalamine and hydroxycobalamine the most active. B12 is a red, water-soluble crystalline substance (the red comes from the cobalt atom), slowly destroyed by acid, alkali, light and oxidizing/reducing agents — and about 30% of its activity is lost in cooking. It was isolated from liver extracts in 1948 and shown to have anti-pernicious-anemia activity.
claims.verbatim:
B12 cobalt is chelated in a large tetrapyrrole ring
similar to the porphyrin ring found in hemoglobin (iron) and
chlorophyll (magnesium).

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: How do animals get vitamin B12 from cobalt?
claims.answer_short: Microbes do the work: gut bacteria in a cow's rumen turn elemental cobalt into B12, which the animal absorbs. Carnivores get it secondhand from prey, and rabbits and rodents eat their own night feces (coprophagy) to recover it.
claims.answer: Wallach explains how animals actually get their B12 from elemental cobalt — a job done by microbes, not the animal itself. Ruminants (cows, sheep, goats, deer, antelope, buffalo, giraffe) rely on the microbes fermenting plant material in their first stomach (the rumen) to convert elemental cobalt into vitamin B12, which the animal then absorbs. Carnivores get their B12 secondhand by eating the stomach contents, liver, bone and muscle of their ruminant prey. And poultry, lagomorphs (rabbits and hares) and rodents eat feces at night (coprophagy) to recover the B12 their own gut microbes manufactured.
claims.verbatim:
Ruminants (i.e. cows, sheep, goats, deer, antelope,
buffalo, giraffe, etc.) can use elemental cobalt because the
microbes fermenting and digesting plant material in their first
stomach (rumen) convert elemental cobalt into vitamin B12,
which the animal then uses.

claims.subject: diabetes
claims.question: How does chromium deficiency lead to diabetes?
claims.answer_short: Chromium runs the body's blood-sugar handling; deficiency wrecks glucose tolerance (77% of 'normal' over-70s) — and Wallach cites the USDA that 90% of Americans are chromium-deficient.
claims.answer: Wallach ties chromium deficiency straight to the body's handling of blood sugar. Pregnant women run lower fasting plasma chromium than non-pregnant women, and the well-documented worsening of glucose tolerance during a 'normal' pregnancy reflects that deficiency — which, he says, often tips over into pregnancy-onset (gestational) diabetes. He frames it as widespread and worsening with age: one study found abnormal glucose tolerance in 77% of clinically 'normal' adults over 70, and he cites the USDA's Richard Anderson that 90% of all Americans are chromium-deficient.
claims.verbatim:
The fasting level of plasma chromium is lower in
pregnant women than in non-pregnant women. Increasing
impairment of glucose tolerance in “normal” pregnancy is
well documented and reflects a chromium deficiency that
oftentimes results in pregnancy onset diabetes. One study
demonstrated abnormal glucose tolerance in 77% of clinically
“normal” adults over the age of 70. According to Richard
Anderson of the USDA, “Ninety percent of all Americans are
deficient in chromium.”

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: Why is chromium so easy to lose and hard to absorb?
claims.answer_short: Sugar flushes chromium out in urine (up 300% for 12 hrs) and food chromium is barely retained; form decides - ~25% of chelated vs up to 98% of colloidal is absorbed.
claims.answer: Wallach explains why chromium is both easy to lose and hard to absorb — his argument for supplementing it in a highly-absorbable form. Eating sugar (colas, fruit juices, honey, candy, table sugar, fructose) raises the rate at which chromium is flushed out in the urine by 300% for 12 hours. And ordinary inorganic chromium from food and water is poorly used: a typical 50-100 microgram (mcg) intake yields only 0.25-5 mcg the body can actually retain. Form is decisive — 25% of chelated chromium is absorbed, versus up to 98% of colloidal chromium. He notes the chromium RDA (the government's Recommended Daily Allowance) is 50-200 mcg of usable chromium per day for adults.
claims.verbatim:
Dietary sugar
loads (i.e. colas, apple juice, grape juice, honey, candy, table
sugar, fructose, etc.) increase the natural rate of urinary Cr loss
by 300% for 12 hours. The average intake of 50 to 100 ug of
inorganic chromium from food and water supplies only 0.25
to 5 ug of usable and retainable chromium. By contrast, 25%
of chelated chromium is absorbed and up to 98% of colloidal


 

chromium is absorbed. The chromium RDA for humans is a
range of 50 to 200 ug of usable chromium per day for adults.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: Has Americans' chromium level been falling?
claims.answer_short: Yes - the young hold more chromium than the old, unsupplemented tissue steadily drops with age, and Wallach charts a steep fall in average American blood chromium since 1948.
claims.answer: A recurring worry in the book: Americans' chromium status has been sliding for decades. Newborn animals and people carry more chromium per pound of body weight than older ones, and in anyone who doesn't supplement, tissue chromium steadily falls with age. Wallach flags a population-wide drop in average American blood chromium since 1948, tabulating mean levels in micrograms per liter (mcg/L) by year: 28 in cities and 1000 in rural areas in 1948, 13 in 1971, 10 in 1972, 4.7-5.1 in 1973, 0.73-1.6 in 1974, 0.16 in 1978, 0.43 in 1980, and 0.13 by 1985.
claims.verbatim:
The concentration of chromium found in newborn
animals and humans is higher per pound of body weight
than it is in older individuals. In fact, the chromium levels of
unsupplemented human tissue, steadily decreases throughout
life. Of greater concern has been the steady decline in the
average American serum chromium since 1948.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: How was chromium discovered, and why does it color gemstones?
claims.answer_short: Found in 1797 by Vauquelin and named from Greek 'chroma' (color) for its vivid compounds - trace chromium makes rubies red, emeralds green, and alexandrite shift color.
claims.answer: The element's backstory — and why it colors gemstones. Chromium was discovered by the French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin in 1797 and named from the Greek chroma, 'color,' because all its compounds display a color (the pure metal itself, though, is a hard, brittle, silver-white). Added to steel at 18% it makes stainless steel, and its almost-invisible oxide layer makes it extremely resistant to corrosion — the decorative, protective plating on bathroom fixtures, jewelry and car bumpers. Trace chromium is what tints many gems: it makes rubies red (in corundum), emeralds green (in beryl), and gives alexandrite (in chrysoberyl) its color-shift — red in firelight, blue in daylight.
claims.verbatim:
Chromium was discovered by French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin in 1797 and named from the Greek word
chroma, which translates to “color.”

claims.subject: obscure_elements
claims.question: How was cesium discovered?
claims.answer_short: In 1860 the German chemists Bunsen and Kirchhoff identified cesium by its spectral 'fingerprint' -- the colors of light it emits when heated. Its lines were sky-blue, so they named it from the Latin caesius, 'sky blue.'
claims.answer: The element's discovery story. Cesium was discovered in 1860 by the German chemists Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff, who isolated it by observing its spectral 'fingerprint' — the specific colors of light (spectral emission lines) it emits when heated. Those lines were bright blue, which is why they named it cesium, from the Latin caesius ('sky blue').
claims.verbatim:
Cesium was discovered in 1860 by the German chemists
Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff. They isolated cesium by
observing colors or spectral emission lines, that cesium emits
when it is heated. The color lines were bright blue, which
prompted them to name the element cesium after the Latin
coesius (“sky blue”).

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: What is copper, and where does its name come from?
claims.answer_short: A soft reddish metal - only 0.007% of Earth's crust. Its name is Latin 'cuprum' ('from Cyprus,' where Rome mined it), and it was one of humanity's first metals.
claims.answer: The element's name and history. Copper makes up only 0.007% of the earth's crust. Its name comes from the Latin cuprum, meaning 'from Cyprus' — the Romans mined their copper on the island of Cyprus. Copper was one of the first metals humanity used: copper jewelry dating back to 9000 B.C. has been found in Iraq. Because pure copper is soft, ancient peoples alloyed it with tin to make bronze, zinc to make brass, and nickel to make monel, producing harder metals for tools and weapons.
claims.verbatim:
Despite the common use of copper, it makes up only
0.007% of the earth’s crust. Copper gets its name from the
Latin word, cuprum, which translates to “from Cyprus,” a
reference to the fact that the Romans mined their copper from
the island of Cyprus.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: What are normal copper levels in the blood?
claims.answer_short: Average plasma copper is about 87-153 (women) and 89-137 (men) micrograms per deciliter, and ~90% of it rides on a carrier protein called ceruloplasmin.
claims.answer: Typical copper levels in the blood. Wallach gives average plasma copper as 87–153 mg/dl (women) and 89–137 mg/dl (men). About 90% of the copper in plasma travels bound to a carrier protein called ceruloplasmin.
claims.verbatim:
The average plasma copper levels of women ranges
from 87 to 153 mg/dl; for men the range is 89 to 137 mg/dl.
About 90% of the plasma copper is bound in a protein called
ceruloplasmin.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: What raises blood copper, and what is copper overload?
claims.answer_short: Copper roughly doubles in pregnancy and on the pill, and rises with infection, liver disease and pellagra; overload shows as copper Kayser-Fleischer rings in the eye.
claims.answer: Some situations that raise blood copper. Serum and plasma copper roughly double (increase 100%) in pregnant women and in women taking oral contraceptives (the pill), and rise during acute infections, liver disease, and pellagra (the disease of niacin / vitamin-B3 deficiency). When copper accumulates in the cornea of the eye it forms visible Kayser-Fleischer rings — a classic sign of copper overload.
claims.verbatim:
Serum and plasma copper increases 100% in pregnant
women and women using oral contraceptives. Serum copper
levels are also elevated during acute infections, liver disease,
and pellagra (niacin deficiency).

Accumulations of copper in the cornea form Kayser-Fleischer Rings.

claims.subject: rare_earth_elements
claims.question: What is dysprosium?
claims.answer_short: A soft, silvery rare-earth metal -- the 9th most abundant of the rare earths -- discovered in 1886 and named from the Greek for 'hard to get at.' Its magnetic alloys help CDs work, and in the body it collects in bone.
claims.answer: Dysprosium is a rare earth element and, Wallach notes, the ninth most abundant of the rare earths. It was discovered in 1886 by the French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran while working with a sample of erbium oxide, and named from the Greek dysprositos — 'hard to get at.' It's a soft, shiny, silvery metal (soft enough to cut with a knife) that is fairly stable in air, and its magnetic alloys are used to help compact discs (CDs) work efficiently. In the body it accumulates in the bones.
claims.verbatim:
Of the rare earths, dysprosium is a metal that ranks
ninth in abundance. It was discovered in 1886 by the French
chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran who was working
with a sample of erbium oxide. It was named for the Greek
word dysprositos, which translates to “hard to get at.”

claims.subject: rare_earth_elements
claims.question: What is erbium used for?
claims.answer_short: A scarce rare-earth metal (found 1843), alloyed with vanadium to improve workability; its most memorable use is tinting glass and enamel pink -- the pink glass of sunglasses and costume jewelry. In the body it settles in bone.
claims.answer: Erbium is a scarce rare earth metal, discovered in 1843 by the Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander; in its ores it occurs as an impurity among the other rare earths. Industrially, erbium is alloyed with metals like vanadium to improve their workability, and — its most memorable use — it is added to glass and enamel to tint them pink, the pink glass being used for sunglasses and costume jewelry. In the body it concentrates mainly in bone.
claims.verbatim:
Erbium is employed in special alloys with metals such
as vanadium to improve their workability characteristics.
Erbium is frequently added to glass and enamel to tint them
pink, this glass is commonly used for sunglasses and costume
jewelry.

claims.subject: rare_earth_elements
claims.question: What is europium?
claims.answer_short: One of the rarest rare earths, isolated in 1901 and named for Europe; it is the softest of them and so reactive it bursts into flame in air above 150C. It is mined from the ores monazite and bastnasite.
claims.answer: Europium is a 'light' rare earth and one of the rarest of all the rare earth elements. It was isolated in 1901 by the French chemist Eugène-Anatole Demarçay, who named it for the continent of Europe. It is the softest of the rare earths and ignites spontaneously in air above 150°C. It occurs in the ores monazite and bastnäsite — monazite (found in the river sands of India and Brazil and in Florida beach sand) carries all the rare earths plus thorium and calcium, and large bastnäsite deposits sit in Southern California.
claims.verbatim:
Europium is one of the most-rare of the rare earth
elements. It was isolated in 1901 by the French chemist
Eugene-Anatole Demarcay, who named the new element for
the continent of Europe.

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: What is fluorine?
claims.answer_short: The smallest, lightest and most reactive halogen ('salt former') - a pale-yellow gas so reactive it never occurs free, locked instead in minerals like fluorite.
claims.answer: Fluorine is a halogen — the family Wallach calls the 'salt formers,' which also includes chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine. These elements react by grabbing electrons from other atoms and readily combine with metals to make salts. Fluorine is the smallest, lightest and most reactive of the whole family — a pale-yellow gas whose molecules pair up into two atoms (diatomic), and so reactive it never occurs free in nature; it's found instead locked in minerals like fluorite (calcium fluoride, also called fluorspar).
claims.verbatim:
Fluorine is a member of the halogen family or “salt
formers.” The other members are chlorine, bromine, iodine
and astatine. All halogen atoms react chemically by accepting
electrons from other atoms and easily combine with metals
to form compounds known as salts. Fluorine is the smallest,
lightest and most reactive member of the halogen family.

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: Who discovered fluorine, and what does its name mean?
claims.answer_short: Henri Moissan won the 1906 Nobel Prize for first isolating pure fluorine (1886), after 75 years of effort; the name is Latin 'fluere,' to flow.
claims.answer: The element's discovery. The French chemist Henri Moissan won the 1906 Nobel Prize for being the first to produce fluorine in its pure elemental form — the culmination of 75 years of effort by many chemists, with Moissan finally isolating it in 1886. The name comes from the Latin fluere, 'to flow.'
claims.verbatim:
The French chemist Henri Moissan won the Nobel
Prize in 1906 for being the first to produce fluorine in its pure
elemental form. The name fluorine is derived from the Latin
word fluere, which translates to “to flow.”

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: Is fluoride an essential nutrient?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says yes in trace amounts - before 1972 it was only 'considered' essential for tooth enamel, then Schwarz proved it essential for animals and humans.
claims.answer: Wallach's stance on fluoride's essentiality. Before 1972 fluoride was only 'considered' essential in animals, based on its apparent benefit to tooth enamel in warding off cavities. Then in 1972, Schwarz proved that fluoride was in fact an essential mineral for both animals and humans. (Note: despite this, fluoride is not carried in this system's operational list of Wallach/Youngevity supplement essentials — see the full fluoride stance for why the picture is two-sided.)
claims.verbatim:
Prior to 1972, fluoride was considered essential in
animals because of its apparent benefit for tooth enamel in
warding off dental caries (“cavities”). In 1972, Schwarz proved
that fluoride was in fact an essential mineral for animals and
humans.

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: How much fluoride is in and around us?
claims.answer_short: An adult skeleton can bank up to 2.6 g of fluoride, and the average American takes in ~4.4 mg a day from food, water, toothpaste and supplements combined.
claims.answer: How much fluoride is in and around us. The skeleton of an adult man can hold up to 2.6 grams (2,600 mg) of fluoride in reserve, and the average American takes in 4.4 mg per day from the combination of food, water, toothpaste and nutritional supplements.
claims.verbatim:
The skeletal reserves of fluoride in an adult man can
reach 2.6 gm (2,600 mg); the average daily intake by Americans
is 4.4 mg from combined sources of food, water, toothpaste
and nutritional supplements.

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: How widespread is water fluoridation?
claims.answer_short: About 10,000 U.S. towns fluoridate water at 1 mg/L for 100 million people, reportedly cutting cavities 60-70% - but naturally high levels mottle children's teeth.
claims.answer: The scale of U.S. water fluoridation and its trade-off. About 10,000 American towns and cities — serving 100 million people — add fluoride to municipal drinking water at 1 mg/L (one part per million), which has reportedly cut dental cavities by 60 to 70%. But in certain western U.S. states there is an excess of fluoride — 10 to 45 ppm — with the visible result of mottled (fluorosis-stained) teeth in children.
claims.verbatim:
Approximately 10,000 American towns and cities
serving a total of 100 million people have added fluoride to
their municipal drinking water at the rate of 1 mg/L, which
has reportedly reduced dental caries by 60 to 70%. In certain
western states in the U.S., there is an excess of fluoride,
reaching levels of 10 to 45 ppm with a resultant mottling of
teeth in children.

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: Is fluoridated water safe?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls it 'still highly controversial' - laying out both the cavity benefit and the fluorosis, bone-fracture and cancer concerns without a flat verdict.
claims.answer: Wallach's full stance on fluoride — why it sounds both essential and dangerous, made clear. WHAT IT IS: fluoride is the most reactive halogen and, per a 1972 study by Schwarz, a nutritionally essential trace mineral for animals and humans. ITS REAL BENEFIT: fluoride hardens tooth enamel — teeth rebuild it as acid-resistant fluorapatite, which fights the cavities caused by sugar-fed mouth bacteria; that is why it's in toothpaste, and water fluoridation (~1 mg/L) has reportedly cut cavities 60–70%. ITS REAL HARMS: fluoride is also toxic above trace levels — dental fluorosis (mottled teeth) at 2–7 ppm, osteosclerosis (abnormal bone hardening) at 8–20 ppm, and chronic systemic toxicity above 20–80 ppm/day over years — and Wallach cites studies (Yiamouyiannis & Burk 1977; the U.S. National Toxicology Program's 1990 rat study) tying fluoridation to excess cancer deaths and to oral, bone (osteosarcoma), thyroid and liver tumors. HOW IT'S BOTH — the reconciliation: the dose makes the poison. Fluoride is essential only in tiny amounts (skeletal reserves in an adult man can reach 2.6 g; the average daily intake by Americans is 4.4 mg), while the harms appear at higher, sustained exposure — so 'essential in trace' and 'toxic in excess' are the same mineral at different doses, not a contradiction. ON WATER FLUORIDATION: Wallach calls it 'still highly controversial' and presents both sides — the cavity benefit versus the fluorosis, bone and cancer concerns, even noting that studies disagree on whether fluoridated water reduces or increases bone fractures. In this passage he lays out the debate and flags the toxicity/cancer evidence rather than issuing a flat yes-or-no verdict on whether you should drink it.
claims.verbatim:
The universal fluoridation of drinking water is still
highly controversial. Some studies show that fluoridated
water helps reduce fractures from osteoporosis, while other
studies showed an increase in hip fractures.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What is iron, and where does it come from?
claims.answer_short: Iron is the 4th most abundant element in Earth's crust — its ores opened the Iron Age (~1100 B.C.), and Earth's molten core is thought to be magnetized iron.
claims.answer: How abundant iron is, and its place in human history. Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust and the second most abundant metal (after aluminum); its content is responsible for most soil color, and the planet's molten core is thought to be magnetized iron. Learning to smelt iron from its red-brown ores (mainly hematite and magnetite) was a milestone that opened the Iron Age (~1100 B.C.), giving humanity tools and weapons harder than those of the earlier Bronze Age; today iron makes up about 90% of all metal extracted from ore.
claims.verbatim:
Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the earth’s
crust and is second only to aluminum as the most abundant
metal. The “core” or interior of the earth is theorized to be
made up of magnetized, molten iron.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: Why is carbon monoxide so deadly?
claims.answer_short: Carbon monoxide binds the iron in hemoglobin ~200x more tightly than oxygen — crowding oxygen out of the blood, which is what makes it poisonous.
claims.answer: Why carbon monoxide is so deadly — it hijacks iron's oxygen seat. Carbon monoxide, a gas produced by incomplete burning of fuel, binds to the iron in hemoglobin 200 times more tightly than oxygen does. Because it clings so hard, it crowds oxygen out of the blood — which is what makes carbon monoxide poisoning dangerous.
claims.verbatim:
Carbon monoxide, a byproduct of imperfect
combustion, is bound to the hemoglobin iron 200 times more
tightly than oxygen - this phenomenon can lead to “carbon
monoxide poisoning!”

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: How much iron is in your body, and where?
claims.answer_short: A healthy adult carries 3-5 g of iron; ~60-70% is 'functional' (in hemoglobin, muscle and enzymes) and 30-40% is stored in marrow and liver.
claims.answer: How much iron your body holds, and where it sits. A healthy adult carries about 3 to 5 grams of iron, and a newborn has nearly twice as much per kilogram of body weight as an adult. Roughly 60 to 70% is 'functional' iron doing active work — in hemoglobin, in muscle's oxygen-storing pigment myoglobin, and in the cell's respiratory enzymes — while 30 to 40% is held in reserve as storage iron (as ferritin and hemosiderin in the bone marrow and liver).
claims.verbatim:
In a healthy adult human there is three to five grams
of iron, the newborn infant has nearly double the amount of
iron per kg than adults. Sixty to 70% of tissue iron is used as
essential or functional iron, and 30 to 40% as storage iron.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What causes iron deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's list: unsupplemented pregnancy, heavy periods, chronic infection or bleeding, low stomach acid, diarrhea, and poor absorption from high-fiber diets.
claims.answer: What causes iron deficiency in the first place. Wallach lists the drivers: an unsupplemented pregnancy; painful menstruation (dysmenorrhea); chronic infections; low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria, e.g. from a salt-restricted diet); chronic diarrhea; ongoing blood loss (from cancer, ulcers, parasites, blood-thinning drugs, or other nutritional deficiencies); and poor absorption (from high-fat or high-fiber diets, or celiac disease).
claims.verbatim:
Iron deficiency can be the result of unsupplemented
pregnancy, dysmenorrhea, chronic infections, hypochlorhydria
(low stomach acid from a salt-restricted diet), chronic diarrhea,
chronic bleeding (i.e. cancer, ulcers, parasites, blood thinners,
nutritional deficiencies, etc.) and impaired absorption (i.e.
high fat diets, high fiber diets, celiac disease, etc.).

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What helps or blocks iron absorption?
claims.answer_short: Stomach acid and vitamin C boost iron absorption; fiber and phytates block it — so Wallach says the 18 mg RDA is too low for vegans and high-fiber diets.
claims.answer: What helps and hinders iron absorption — and why the standard allowance can fall short. Stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) is needed to absorb iron well, and vitamin C (ascorbic acid) increases absorption; clays and dietary fiber (phytates) reduce it. Because of that, Wallach argues the official RDA (Recommended Dietary Allowance) of 18 mg per day of metallic iron is too low for people eating high-fiber, high-phytate diets, such as vegans and vegetarians.
claims.verbatim:
Stomach hydrochloric acid is required for optimal
absorption of iron. Ascorbic acid increases the absorption of
iron; clays and dietary fiber (phytates) decrease the absorption
of iron. The RDA of 18 mg per day as metallic iron is too low
for those individuals consuming high fiber, high phytate diets
(vegans, vegetarians, etc.).

claims.subject: gallium
claims.question: What is gallium - the metal that melts in your hand?
claims.answer_short: A soft, aluminum-like metal so low-melting it liquefies from your body heat, yet has the widest liquid range of any metal; named for Gallia (the Latin name for France).
claims.answer: Gallium — the metal that melts in your hand. Gallium is in the same chemical family as aluminum and behaves much like it. It is so soft you can cut it with a knife, and its melting point is so low (29.8 degrees C, about 86 degrees F) that it turns liquid from the warmth of your hand; yet it does not boil until 2,403 degrees C, giving it the widest liquid range of any known metal. Its existence was predicted by Mendeleyev's periodic table in 1871, and Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran identified it in 1875, naming it for Gallia (the Latin name for France).
claims.verbatim:
It is an extremely soft metal that can easily be cut with a knife.
It also has an extremely low melting point of 29.8 degrees C,
allowing gallium to liquefy when it is held in the hand. Gallium
has an extremely high boiling point of 2,403 degrees C, allowing
gallium to be in its liquid form in a range greater than that of
any known metal.

claims.subject: gallium
claims.question: Is gallium used in cancer medicine?
claims.answer_short: Yes - gallium-67 (78-hour half-life), one of medicine's first man-made isotopes, gathers in cancers like melanoma, letting it treat them without damage to surrounding tissues.
claims.answer: Gallium-67 in cancer medicine. Gallium-67 was one of the first artificially produced radioactive isotopes used in medicine. Its short half-life (78 hours) means it quickly loses its radioactivity and its tissue-destroying power. Because gallium-67 tends to accumulate in certain cancers (such as melanoma), it can be used to treat those cancers without damage to the surrounding healthy tissue.
claims.verbatim:
radioactive isotopes to be used in medicine. Because of its
short half-life (78 hours), it rapidly loses its radioactivity and
its destructive properties. This isotope has the property of
accumulating in certain cancers (melanoma) and is used to
treat these cancers without damage to surrounding tissues.

claims.subject: rare_earth_elements
claims.question: Where is gadolinium found?
claims.answer_short: A rare-earth mineral scattered through rocks and plants -- hickory trees can concentrate it to 70 ppm -- and in land animals it collects in the bone and liver almost as soon as it is absorbed.
claims.answer: Gadolinium — a rare-earth mineral. Wallach notes where gadolinium turns up in nature (rocks, and plants — the hickory genus Carya can concentrate it to 70 ppm), and that in land animals it collects in the bone and liver almost immediately after it is absorbed.
claims.verbatim:
Gd-Gadolinium, a rare earth, is found in igneous rocks
at 5.4 ppm, shale at 4.3 ppm, sandstone at 2.6 ppm, limestone
at 0.7 ppm, terrestrial plants (Carya spp.) can concentrate
gadolinium up to 70 ppm, and in marine animals at 0.06 ppm.
Terrestrial animals accumulate gadolinium in bone and liver
almost immediately after absorption.

claims.subject: germanium
claims.question: What is germanium?
claims.answer_short: A metalloid 'semiconductor' element predicted by Mendeleyev in 1871 and isolated in 1886 - 'doped' with a trace of arsenic or gallium, it makes transistors.
claims.answer: Germanium — the semiconductor element. Its existence (as 'eka-silicon') was predicted by Mendeleyev's 1871 periodic table, but it was not actually isolated until 1886, by the German scientist Clemens Winkler. Germanium is a poor conductor of electricity, which makes it a semiconductor; adding tiny amounts of arsenic, gallium or antimony ('doping') sharply increases its conductivity, and doped germanium is used to make transistors — essentially micro-computers.
claims.verbatim:
The existence of the “metalloid” element germanium or
eka-silicon, had been predicted by Mendeleyev in his periodic
table in 1871, however, it was not until 1886 that Clemens
Winkler, a German scientist, isolated the silicon-like element
germanium. Germanium is a poor conductor of electricity
and therefore is relegated to a semi-conductor status.

claims.subject: germanium
claims.question: How does germanium behave in the body?
claims.answer_short: It accepts and passes electrons like a semiconductor; biologically Wallach calls it an 'electrical impulse initiator' in cells and a cofactor for oxygen use.
claims.answer: How germanium behaves — from radios to cells. In the 1940s-50s, germanium diode crystals were used in do-it-yourself radio kits because the germanium atom readily accepts and transmits electrons, acting as a semiconductor. It is chemically close to silica and carbon, and biologically Wallach describes germanium as a highly effective 'electrical impulse initiator' inside cells and a metallic cofactor (helper mineral) for the body's use of oxygen.
claims.verbatim:
The germanium atom is structured so it accepts and
transmits electrons effectively acting as a semiconductor. It is
not too surprising that germanium is closely related to silica
and carbon. Biologically, germanium is a highly effective
electrical impulse initiator intracellularly and acts as a metallic
cofactor for oxygen utilization.

claims.subject: germanium
claims.question: How was germanium's healing reputation discovered?
claims.answer_short: In 1950 the Japanese chemist Dr. Kazuhiko Asai found germanium in fossilized plants, and Russian researchers soon attributed anti-cancer activity to it.
claims.answer: The research that put germanium on the map (background, for information). In 1950 the Japanese chemist Dr. Kazuhiko Asai found traces of germanium in fossilized plant life, and Russian researchers soon attributed anti-cancer activity to germanium. This reports the Asai/Russian research that Wallach cites; germanium's operational deficiency-to-cancer link is carried separately by the germanium-deficiency claim.

In 1950, Dr. Kazuhiko Asai, a Japanese chemist, found
traces of germanium in fossilized plantlife. Russian researchers
quickly attributed anti-cancer activity to germanium.

claims.subject: germanium
claims.question: How does germanium support the immune system?
claims.answer_short: Asai tied germanium-rich herbs to healing; germanium boosts natural killer cells, interferon-gamma, macrophages and T-suppressor cells.
claims.answer: How germanium supports immunity. Dr. Asai tied the healing power of certain herbs to their high germanium content (many are germanium-accumulating plants). Germanium is known to strengthen the immune system by boosting natural killer cells, lymphokines (immune-signaling proteins) such as interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), macrophages, and T-suppressor cells.

system by stimulating the production of natural killer cells,

claims.answer_short: An organic, chelated germanium (carboxyethyl germanium sesquioxide) Asai made in 1967 - absorbed at ~30% and fully excreted within a week.

Asai synthesized Ge-132, carboxyethyl germanium

germanium structure forms a cubic structure with three
negative oxygen ions at the base of a cubic triangle. As an
organic or chelated form of germanium, Ge-132 is absorbed
at the rate of 30% efficiency and the total intake is completely
excreted in one week.

claims.subject: germanium
claims.question: Why are the 'Holy Waters' of Lourdes said to heal?

claims.answer: Wallach's mineral explanation for the 'Holy Waters' of Lourdes. The famous healing waters of Lourdes, France — known worldwide for their reputed healing properties — contain large amounts of germanium and lithium, which Wallach points to as the natural source of their reputation.

The “Holy Waters” at Lourdes, France, known world
wide for their healing properties, contains large amounts of
germanium and lithium.

claims.subject: hydrogen
claims.question: What is hydrogen?
claims.answer_short: The simplest atom -- one proton, one electron -- and the most abundant element in the universe (~93% of all atoms). As a gas it is diatomic (H2), colorless and highly flammable, burning with oxygen to make water; its name is Greek for 'water-maker.'
claims.answer: What hydrogen is. Hydrogen is the simplest atom — a single proton circled by a single electron — which is part of why it is the most abundant element in the universe: it dominates interstellar space and the stars, and makes up 93% of all the atoms in existence. As a gas it is diatomic (two atoms bonded, H2), colorless, odorless, tasteless, and extremely flammable, burning with oxygen to form water (its name comes from the Greek hydro 'water' + genes 'creator').
claims.verbatim:
Hydrogen is the most simple of all atoms, consisting
of a single proton, its nucleus, which is circled by a single
electron. Its simple and basic structure partially explains
why hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe.
Enormous quantities of hydrogen gas is found in interstellar
space, and is by far the most dominant element found in the
stars. Hydrogen atoms make up a whopping 93% of all the
atoms in the universe.

claims.subject: hydrogen
claims.question: Who discovered hydrogen?
claims.answer_short: Henry Cavendish (1731-1810), who made the gas in 1766 - a brilliant, painfully shy recluse who never spoke to women and gave servants orders by written note.
claims.answer: Who discovered hydrogen — and how odd he was. Hydrogen's identification as an element is credited to the English chemist Henry Cavendish (1731-1810), who first produced the gas in 1766 by dropping zinc into hydrochloric acid and recognized the 'inflammable air' as a distinct element (he also accurately calculated the gravitational constant G and the mass of the Earth). Cavendish was famously eccentric: frugal, shy and stuttering, he never spoke directly to women, gave his female servants instructions by written note, and would fire any he saw as he walked through his house.
claims.verbatim:
Cavendish, a frugal, shy, stuttering and eccentric
scientist, was the son of an extremely wealthy English
aristocrat. Cavendish never spoke directly to women; he gave
instructions to his female servants by handwritten letters,
and would summarily fire them if they came into his line of
sight as he walked through his laboratory or house. He spent


little of his great fortune and spent his entire life buried in his
laboratory “in the pursuit of knowledge.”

claims.subject: hydrogen
claims.question: What does hydrogen have to do with the Hindenburg?
claims.answer_short: Hydrogen's lightness made it the early lift gas for blimps - until a spark ignited the hydrogen-filled Hindenburg in 1937 and the industry switched to helium.
claims.answer: Hydrogen, lifting power, and the Hindenburg. Hydrogen is lighter than air, so a hydrogen-filled balloon rises and drifts away — its low density gives it enormous lifting power, and it was once the main lift gas for manned balloons and blimps. That ended in 1937 when a spark from a grounded docking line set the hydrogen-filled German blimp Hindenburg on fire, prompting the airship industry to abandon flammable hydrogen and switch to non-flammable helium.
claims.verbatim:
Hydrogen was once the main lifting power for
manned balloons and “blimps.” A discharge spark from a
grounded docking line set the hydrogen containing German
blimp, Hindenburg, on fire in 1937, causing the “lighter than
air” airship industry to abandon the gas and switch to the
non-flammable helium.

claims.subject: hydrogen
claims.question: How does hydrogen set the body's acid-base balance?
claims.answer_short: Regulating acid-base balance is really regulating hydrogen-ion (H+) levels - healthy blood is held in a narrow pH band of 7.36-7.44 by homeostatic mechanisms.
claims.answer: Hydrogen and the body's acid-base balance. Seventy percent of the human body is water, and hydrogen is a major constituent of water and of all organic molecules. Wallach's key point: regulating the body's acid-base balance is, in fact, regulating the hydrogen-ion (H+) levels of the fluids inside and around cells. The body holds this acidity within a narrow range through complex self-regulating (homeostatic) mechanisms — the pH of healthy blood runs from 7.36 to 7.44.
